extracted.intended_audience: regulatory economists, DOL analysts, employers, labor-policy stakeholders, and public commenters on the overtime rule
extracted.subtask_description: Quantitative and qualitative methods for estimating transfers, hours, wages, and employer responses to changes in the EAP salary and HCE compensation levels in the DOL overtime rule; includes worker classification, elasticity assumptions, and modeling choices used to project Year‑1 and longer‑run effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hourly rate calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: The hourly rate of pay is calculated as usual weekly earnings divided by usual weekly hours worked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a worker paid $684 per week must work 94.3 hours per week to earn less than the Federal minimum wage of $7.25 per hour ($684 ÷ $7.25 = 94.3). This implicit hourly rate is used to identify workers earning below applicable minimum wages and to compute wage increases needed to reach the minimum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicable minimum wage determination
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicable minimum wage for analysis is the higher of the Federal minimum wage and the state minimum wage as of January 1, 2023.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the jurisdictional (state or federal) higher rate when calculating which workers earn an implicit hourly rate below the minimum and the transfers required to bring wages up to the minimum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfers due to minimum wage provision
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate transfers by calculating the change in earnings if wages rose to the applicable minimum wage for workers who become nonexempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute change in weekly earnings for affected workers and aggregate (e.g., $84.73 × 19,900 = $1.7 million per week, $87.5 million in Year 1). Account for possible employer hour reductions, but assume disemployment effects are negligible when the affected population is small.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated employer responses to updated salary levels
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers may respond to an increase in the regular rate of pay by: (1) paying overtime premiums to affected workers; (2) reducing overtime hours and transferring hours to other workers; (3) reducing the regular rate of pay for affected workers (as long as still above minimum wage); (4) increasing affected workers' salaries to preserve exempt status; or (5) using some combination of these responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modeling must consider the relative costs and likelihood of each response; the chosen behavioral response mix drives transfer estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two conceptual adjustment models (fixed-wage vs fixed-job)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the fixed-wage (labor demand) model and the fixed-job (employment contract) model to conceptualize employer adjustments to overtime eligibility changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fixed-wage: standard hourly wage independent of overtime premium; leads to reduced overtime hours and higher prevalence of 40-hour weeks, with increased earnings for those still working overtime. Fixed-job: standard hourly wage adjusts to offset overtime premium so weekly earnings and hours are unchanged except when prevented by minimum wage. Empirical evidence partly supports each model depending on worker wage relative to minimum wage; use of a hybrid/incomplete fixed-job model may be appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of adjustment model: incomplete fixed-job model
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department adopts an 'incomplete fixed-job' model — a hybrid between the fixed-job and fixed-wage models — because literature suggests wages adjust toward offsetting overtime requirements but not fully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justification: synthesis of Trejo (1991, 2003), Barkume (2010), Bell & Hart (2003), and others; empirical findings indicate partial wage adjustment, especially for above‑minimum-wage workers, and larger effects for minimum‑wage workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling incomplete fixed-job adjustments using Trejo and Barkume estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Model adjustment as the average of Trejo's (1991) estimate (overtime-induced wage change = 40% of fixed-job predicted adjustment assuming initial zero overtime premium) and Barkume's (2010) estimate (80% of predicted adjustment assuming an initial 28% voluntary overtime premium).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This corresponds to assuming salaried overtime workers implicitly receive the equivalent of a 14% overtime premium in the absence of regulation (midpoint between 0 and 28 percent). Use the average of the two adjustment estimates to determine wage change magnitudes for affected workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labor demand elasticity values for hours adjustment
rubrics_metrics.description: Use labor demand elasticities to convert wage changes into changes in hours demanded: short-term elasticity = −0.20 (Year 1); long-term elasticity = −0.40 (Years 2–10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These elasticity choices are informed by literature (e.g., Wolfson & Belman meta-analysis range −0.05 to −0.12 and Lichter et al. (2014)); the Department selected −0.2 and −0.4 consistent with prior rulemakings and to bound short- and long-run effects. Percent change in total hours worked is set equal to percent change in average wages multiplied by the wage elasticity of labor demand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate disemployment effect conservatively/negligibly when affected share is small
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the share of workers affected by minimum wage provision is small (e.g., an estimated 0.5 percent, 19,900 workers), the Department assumes any disemployment effect due to the minimum wage provision will be negligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nevertheless, Year 1 disemployment effects are estimated using a labor demand elasticity of −0.2 (and −0.4 for long run) to bound potential reductions in hours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification into four types of affected workers (Type 1–4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify four worker types to model heterogeneous employer responses: Type 1: workers who do not work overtime; Type 2: workers who do not regularly work overtime but occasionally work overtime; Type 3: workers who regularly work overtime and become overtime-eligible (nonexempt); Type 4: workers who regularly work overtime and remain exempt because raising salary is cheaper for employer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use CPS variables (e.g., PEHRUSL1 > 40) and supplementary SIPP data to classify workers; this taxonomy determines which modeling approach (no change, transfer, incomplete fixed-job adjustments, or salary increase) applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing Type 3 vs Type 4 using expected nonexempt earnings plus managerial costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate each worker's weekly earnings if they became nonexempt, add weekly managerial costs ($14.47 per affected worker), and classify as Type 4 if expected nonexempt earnings plus managerial costs exceeds the updated standard salary level; otherwise classify as Type 3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Managerial cost used: $14.47 = $86.82 per hour × (10 minutes ÷ 60 minutes). The assumption is that firms consider incremental managerial costs when deciding whether to keep a worker exempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification and sizing of Type 2 (occasional overtime) using CPS and SIPP
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify Type 2 workers in two steps: (1) use CPS MORG data to find those who do not usually work overtime but did work overtime in the survey week; (2) supplement with SIPP to estimate annual likelihood of working some overtime (31.3% of non-hourly workers in 2021) and scale the Type 2 population so Type 2+3+4 ≈ 31.3% of affected workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Type 2 is later subdivided into Type 2A (unexpected overtime) and Type 2B (expected occasional overtime) for different modeling treatments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subdivision of Type 2 into Type 2A and Type 2B (50/50 split)
rubrics_metrics.description: Due to uncertainty about the nature of occasional overtime hours, assume 50% of Type 2 workers have unexpected overtime (Type 2A) and 50% have expected overtime (Type 2B); assignment is random.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Type 2A workers: treated as receiving a 50% overtime premium for hours >40 and no change in base wage or hours (full overtime premium model). Type 2B workers: treated like Type 3 (incomplete fixed-job adjustments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of Type 1 and Type 4 in wage/hour modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Type 1 workers (do not work overtime) will become overtime-eligible but see no change in wages, hours, or weekly earnings. Type 4 workers will remain exempt with earnings raised to meet the updated salary or HCE level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is possible employers may increase Type 4 hours in response to higher salary, but lacking data the Department assumes hours do not change for Type 4.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling changes for Type 2B and Type 3 using incomplete fixed-job adjustment
rubrics_metrics.description: For Type 3 and Type 2B workers (those with expected overtime), apply the incomplete fixed-job model to estimate changes in regular hourly wages and hours: wages adjust downward partially and hours decline slightly, while overtime premium for hours >40 results in increased average weekly earnings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute adjusted total hours by setting percent change in hours = percent change in average wages × wage elasticity of labor demand (−0.20 short-term, −0.40 long-term). Also include 50% overtime premium on hours >40 when computing average weekly earnings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annualizing transfers using CPS reference week
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume the CPS reference week is representative of an average week in the year; total annual transfers = 52 × transfers estimated for the reference week, spread over a larger group that includes those who occasionally work overtime but did not in the CPS week.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach assumes weekly patterns observed in CPS are typical; caveats include sampling limitations and that transfers may be distributed across workers not captured in the reference week.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and treatment of survey evidence in modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey results submitted by commenters (e.g., employer surveys) are treated qualitatively and generally not used quantitatively due to issues like insufficient or uncertain sample sizes, missing sampling methodology, and missing magnitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveys may inform plausible responses but are not directly incorporated into transfer estimates unless methodological reliability and representativeness can be established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition and qualitative accounting of unquantified transfers and secondary effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge additional transfers and effects that are not quantified: hours transferred to other workers, reductions in bonuses/benefits, changes in social assistance eligibility (Medicaid, EITC, SNAP, TANF, WIC, school meals), and resulting changes in government expenditures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss qualitatively how these may increase or decrease household resources and government spending; note the direction of effects depends on the relative magnitudes of earnings changes and assistance value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of alternative empirical studies (e.g., Quach 2022/2024)
rubrics_metrics.description: Review new empirical studies but do not necessarily incorporate them if there are representativeness or methodological limitations (e.g., ADP payroll data not a random sample).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a study has limitations (nonrepresentative sample, unpublished working paper, etc.), the Department may note its findings but retain prior modeling choices unless methodological concerns are resolved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregation and reporting of estimated impacts (counts and dollar transfers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Report estimated number of affected workers by type (e.g., 4.3 million total; 3.0 million Type 1; 704,000 Type 2; 558,800 Type 3; 94,100 Type 4) and aggregate transfer estimates (e.g., Year 1 transfers of $1.5 billion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide tables showing mean hourly wages, usual weekly hours, weekly earnings by type (Tables 11, 14–16) and clearly attribute components of transfers (minimum wage effects, overtime pay provision effects, HCE changes).
